title: Scope of practice, protected titles and referral boundaries
audience: Consultants and coaches who want to offer general information and habit support about everyday eating, and who need to know what that work does not include.
learningOutcomes: Describe the difference between general eating-habit support and the clinical work that belongs to a registered health professional.
Identify the titles you must not use unless you hold the qualification and registration they require.
Recognise the client situations that must be referred on rather than handled in a general consult.
State the limits of a consult clearly to a client before any plan is discussed.

instruction.heading: What this course covers and what it does not
instruction.body: This course covers general information about everyday eating and habit support: shopping, planning, cooking routines, portion awareness at a general level, and helping a client set realistic habit goals. It does not cover diagnosing a condition, treating a disease, prescribing a diet for a medical problem, ordering or interpreting clinical tests, or advising on medication. Those activities sit with registered health professionals. The line between general support and clinical nutrition care is the most important boundary in this course. Where exactly that line falls in your jurisdiction is a question for the qualified reviewer named for this course, and this draft does not settle it. Until the reviewer has confirmed the boundary, treat every client question about a health condition as outside general consulting.

instruction.heading: Protected titles and how you describe yourself
instruction.body: Some titles related to nutrition are restricted. Words such as dietitian and nutritionist may be protected, and the rules differ by country and by state or territory. The protected status, the exact wording allowed, and any registration body that applies have not been confirmed in this draft and are an open question for the qualified reviewer. Until that review is complete, do not use the words dietitian, nutritionist or any close variant in a course title, a business name, a website, a business card, a social media profile or a client message, unless you hold the qualification and registration that the title requires. Describe the service in plain words, such as general eating-habit support, and say clearly what it does not include. Do not imply that completing this course gives you a title, a registration or authority to give clinical advice.

instruction.heading: Client situations that need referral
instruction.body: Some client situations are outside general consulting and must be referred on before any plan is discussed. These include a diagnosed medical condition that diet is expected to manage or treat, a current medication where food or supplements may interact, pregnancy or breastfeeding, a child or adolescent, a request for a therapeutic or medically supervised diet, a history of or current concern about an eating disorder, and any client who describes symptoms they have not yet had checked. The full list, the referral route and the wording of the referral are not confirmed in this draft. Treat this list as a working guide that the qualified reviewer must confirm or replace. When in doubt, pause the consult and refer. Referral is a safe outcome and is not a failure of the service.

instruction.heading: Stating the limits of the service
instruction.body: At the first contact, tell the client what the service is and is not. Say that you provide general information and habit support, that you do not diagnose or treat, that you do not prescribe diets for medical conditions, and that you will refer them to a health professional when a question is outside your scope. Record that you gave this explanation and that the client understood it. This protects the client, who knows what to expect, and it protects you, because the boundary was stated before any advice was given. Do not let a client's request for a quick answer override the limit. A short, clear statement at the start is better than an apology later.

instruction.heading: Verification and escalation
instruction.body: A supervisor or the qualified reviewer should check that the service description, the title wording and the referral list match what the business is allowed to offer. A competent practitioner can name the titles they must not use, explain the boundary between general support and clinical care, list the referral situations and state the limits at the first contact. Escalate to the business owner and the qualified reviewer any request that asks you to use a restricted title, to manage a medical condition, or to offer a diet for a client with a referral situation.

procedure: Read the service description and confirm it matches the approved wording for this business.
Check that no restricted title appears in your profile, marketing, documents or messages.
At the first contact, state what the service is, what it is not, and when you will refer on.
Ask the client about any diagnosed condition, medication, pregnancy or relevant history before discussing any plan.
If a referral situation is present, stop the consult, explain the referral in plain words and record it.
Record the limits statement and the client's acknowledgement in the client file.

workedExamples.situation: A prospective client says they have been told by their doctor to change their diet to manage a diagnosed condition, and asks you to write them a meal plan.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you say, and what do you do next?
workedExamples.reasoning: A diet to manage a diagnosed condition is outside general consulting. Explain that you cannot provide that plan, and suggest they ask their treating doctor for a referral to a registered health professional who can provide clinical nutrition care. Do not write a meal plan, do not name a diet that will treat the condition, and record the referral. Refer the question on the business's escalation route if the client pushes back.

workedExamples.situation: A new client's business card and website say 'Nutritionist' and the owner asks you to keep the same wording on your new profile.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do before you publish the profile?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not publish the restricted title until the qualified reviewer has confirmed what wording is allowed and you hold the qualification the title requires. Raise it with the business owner in writing and use the plain service description meanwhile. This is an open question for the reviewer, and the lesson does not decide it.

equipmentAndPpe: Approved service description and limits statement for the business
Current referral list, once confirmed by the qualified reviewer
Client intake form with a limits acknowledgement field
Private space for the first conversation

commonErrors.error: Using a restricted title in a profile, a flyer or a message because it is common in the industry.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the plain service description until the reviewer confirms the wording and you hold the qualification the title requires.

commonErrors.error: Giving a meal plan to a client who has disclosed a medical condition, to be helpful.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop the plan, explain the limit and refer the client to a registered health professional.

commonErrors.error: Skipping the limits statement because the client is in a hurry.
commonErrors.prevention: Make the statement at every first contact, and record that it was given and understood.

commonErrors.error: Treating the course as permission to give clinical advice.
commonErrors.prevention: State in the lesson and in client communication that completing this course does not give a registration, a title or authority to give clinical advice.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Protected titles for nutrition and dietetics, and the registration that applies to them, vary by jurisdiction. The rules have not been confirmed in this draft. The qualified reviewer must confirm them before the course is published.
Completing this lesson does not grant a registration, a licence, a title or authority to give clinical nutrition advice, to diagnose or to treat any condition.
Advertising and consumer law may apply to claims made about the service. The applicable rules are UNCONFIRMED in this draft and must be checked by the reviewer.

qualityStandard: The limits statement was given at the first contact and recorded with the client's acknowledgement.
No restricted title appears in any material the practitioner controls, unless the qualification and registration it requires are held.
Every referral situation found in the intake was stopped and referred, and the referral was recorded.
No meal plan or clinical advice was given for a client with a referral situation.
documentationEvidence: Signed or acknowledged limits statement in the client file.
Record of any referral, with the reason and the date.
Copy of the service description used at the first contact.
summary: General eating-habit support is different from clinical nutrition care, and the line between them must be confirmed by a qualified reviewer.
Do not use restricted titles unless you hold the qualification and registration they require.
Refer medical conditions, medications, pregnancy, children and eating-disorder concerns rather than handling them in a general consult.
State the limits of the service at the first contact and record it.

knowledgeChecks.question: A client with a diagnosed condition asks for a meal plan to manage it. What is the right first response?
options: Write a simple meal plan, since general eating advice is always safe to give
Explain the limit of the service and refer the client to a registered health professional, recording the referral.
Ask the client to try a popular diet for two weeks and report back on how they feel

knowledgeChecks.question: Which is the safest approach to a restricted title while the reviewer has not confirmed the wording?
options: Use the title in marketing, since most clients will not check the rules
Describe the service in plain words and do not use restricted titles until the wording is confirmed and the qualification is held.
Add the word 'trainee' before the restricted title so it is clear you are not yet qualified

knowledgeChecks.question: Why state the service limits at the first contact?
options: So the client knows what to expect, and the boundary is clear before any advice is given.
So the client pays a higher fee for the consult
So the practitioner can avoid keeping any client notes
